## Polished Markdown

Let $x>0$ and $y\in\mathbb{R}$. Define
$$
r=\frac{y}{x}.
$$
Since $x>0$, this is a real number. By the Archimedean property, there exists
$n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>r$. Multiplying by the positive number $x$
preserves the inequality, so
$$
nx>rx=\frac{y}{x}x=y.
$$
Therefore there exists $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $nx>y$.

cor:archimedean-reciprocal.title: The Reciprocal Sequence Converges to Zero (proof-2026-07-31-001)
cor:archimedean-reciprocal.body:
Correct epsilon proof of 1/n -> 0 using the Archimedean property: choose N > 1/epsilon, then for n >= N obtain 0 < 1/n <= 1/N < epsilon.

Tags: handwritten, correct, staging
cor:archimedean-reciprocal.ocr_text:
A := {1/n : n in N}.

lim_{n -> infinity} 1/n = 0.

By definition this means there exists N in N such that whenever n >= N,
|1/n - 0| < epsilon.

Let epsilon > 0 be arbitrary. By the Archimedean property, there exists N in N such that
N > 1/epsilon.

Then for every n >= N, we have
n >= N > 1/epsilon.

Taking reciprocals gives
1/n <= 1/N < epsilon.

Hence
|1/n - 0| = 1/n < epsilon.

Since this holds for every epsilon > 0, it follows that
1/n -> 0 as n -> infinity.
So the sequence converges and its limit is 0.

cor:multiplicative-cancellation-on-q.title: Multiplicative Cancellation on $\mathbb{Q}$ (proof-2026-07-31-001)
cor:multiplicative-cancellation-on-q.body:
Correct field-level cancellation argument: multiply ac=bc on the right by c^{-1} and use associativity, inverse, and identity laws; specializes to the rational corollary.

Tags: handwritten, correct, staging
cor:multiplicative-cancellation-on-q.ocr_text:
Rational Proofs

Thm: Multiplication Cancellation.
Let F be a field. Let a,b,c in F with c != 0.
Then if ac = bc, then a = b.

Proof. Since F is a field, c has a multiplicative inverse.

ac . (1/c) = bc . (1/c)

a = b.

cor:negation-of-product-on-q.title: Negation of a Product on $\mathbb{Q}$ (proof-2026-07-31-001)
cor:negation-of-product-on-q.body:
Handwritten generic field proof of the identities (-a)b=-(ab) and a(-b)=-(ab). Correct for the rational corollary by specialization to Q, using distributivity, multiplicative identity, and additive inverse uniqueness.

Tags: handwritten, field-algebra, rationals
cor:negation-of-product-on-q.ocr_text:
Theorem. Negation of a product.
Let F be a field and let a,b in F. Then
    -(a b) = (-a)b = a(-b).

Proof.
-(a b) =
    -1(a b)
  = ((-1)a)b
  = (-a)b.

Similarly,
    -(a b) = a((-1)b) = a(-b).

cor:power-of-power-on-q.title: Power of a Power on $\mathbb{Q}$ (proof-2026-07-31-002)
cor:power-of-power-on-q.body:
Handwritten induction attempt for (q^a)^b=q^{ab}. It gives the base case and visible successor step, but only for nonnegative b; the indexed corollary is for all integer exponents m,n, so negative exponent cases and supporting inverse-power laws are missing. Related to the earlier attempt for this route.

Tags: handwritten, rationals, powers, incomplete, duplicate-family
cor:power-of-power-on-q.ocr_text:
Rational proofs.

Theorem. Power of a power in a field.
Let F be a field. Let q in F \ {0}, and let a,b in Z. Then
    (q^a)^b = q^{ab}.

Proof.
Proceed by induction.

Base case:
    (q^a)^0 = 1.

Inductive hypothesis:
    (q^a)^b = q^{ab}.

Show:
    (q^a)^{b+1}
      = (q^a)^b q^a
      = q^{ab} q^a
      = q^{ab+a}.

cor:uniqueness-multiplicative-inverse-on.title: Uniqueness of Multiplicative Inverses on $\mathbb{Q}$ (proof-2026-07-31-001)
cor:uniqueness-multiplicative-inverse-on.body:
Correct field-level inverse uniqueness argument: from ab=1, left-multiply by a^{-1} and use associativity, inverse, and identity laws to get b=a^{-1}; specializes to Q.

Tags: handwritten, correct, staging
cor:uniqueness-multiplicative-inverse-on.ocr_text:
Thm: Uniqueness of Multiplicative Inverse.
Let F be a field and let a in F with a != 0.
If b in F satisfies a . b = 1, then b = a^{-1}.

Proof.
a . b = 1
(a^{-1} . a)b = a^{-1} . 1
b = a^{-1}.

cor:uniqueness-multiplicative-inverse-on.ocr_text:
Theorem. Uniqueness of multiplicative inverse.
Let F be a field and let a in F with a != 0.
If b in F satisfies a b = 1, then b = a^{-1}.

Proof.
ab = 1.
Multiplying by a^{-1},
    a^{-1}(ab) = a^{-1}1.
Thus
    (a^{-1}a)b = a^{-1},
so
    1b = a^{-1}.
Therefore b = a^{-1}.

def:epsilon-characterization-of-infimum.title: Epsilon Characterization of the Infimum (proof-2026-07-31-001)
def:epsilon-characterization-of-infimum.body:
Correct proof of the infimum-to-epsilon-witness direction: if no a in A satisfies a < i+epsilon, then i+epsilon is a lower bound of A above i, contradicting that i is the greatest lower bound.

Tags: handwritten, correct, staging
def:epsilon-characterization-of-infimum.ocr_text:
Lemma. Let A be a nonempty subset of R that is bounded below, and let i = inf A.
Then for every epsilon > 0, there exists a in A such that a < i + epsilon.

Assume for contradiction that for some epsilon > 0, there does not exist an a in A
such that a < i + epsilon. Then for every a in A, i + epsilon <= a.

Thus i + epsilon is a lower bound of A. Since i is the greatest lower bound of A,
we must have i + epsilon <= i.

But epsilon > 0 implies i < i + epsilon, a contradiction.
Therefore there exists a in A such that a < i + epsilon.

def:function-bounded.ocr_text:
Bounded on a Set.

Thm. Let A subset R and let f : A -> R. The function f is said to be bounded
on A if there exists a constant M > 0 such that for all x in A,
  |f(x)| <= M.

Equivalently, f is bounded on A iff there exists M > 0 such that for all
x in A, |f(x)| <= M.

Proof. Let A subset R and let f : A -> R.

If f is bounded on A, then by the LUB/GLB property f has a supremum and
infimum. Let
  s := sup f(x),
  i := inf f(x).
Let M = max(|s|, |i|). Let x in A be arbitrary.
Then
  -M <= i <= f(x) <= s <= M.
Therefore |f(x)| <= M on A.

Conversely, assume |f(x)| <= |M|. Let x in A be arbitrary. Then
  -|M| <= f(x) <= |M|.
Therefore |M| is an upper bound of f(x), and -|M| is a lower bound.
Hence f is bounded on A.

def:reciprocal-on-q-classes.tex:
Rational proofs.

Theorem. Rational reciprocal of a nonzero rational.
For every a,b in Q with a != 0 and b != 0,
(a/b)^{-1} = b/a.

Proof.
Compute:
(a/b)^{-1} * (a/b) = 1.
Also
(b/a)(a/b) = 1.
Therefore
(a/b)^{-1} = b/a.

## Polished Markdown

By the recursive definition of $\WFF$, the negation formation rule says
that whenever $\varphi\in\WFF$, the formula $\neg\varphi$ also belongs
to $\WFF$. Hence
$$
\varphi\in\WFF
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\neg\varphi\in\WFF.
$$
The same definition includes the binary connective formation rule: if
$\varphi,\psi\in\WFF$ and
$$
\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\},
$$
then the composite formula $(\varphi\circ\psi)$ belongs to $\WFF$.
These are exactly the two closure assertions, so $\WFF$ is closed under
the propositional formation rules.

lem:iterator-relation-consistency.ocr_text:
Lemma. Consistency of the minimal iterator relation.
Let (P,S,1) be a Peano system, let (W,c,g) be iterator data for it, and let R* be the minimal iterator relation for (W,c,g). Then R* is an iterator relation for (W,c,g).

Proof.
Define
    I := {R subset P x W | R is an iterator relation for (W,c,g)}.

Define
    R* = intersection over R in I of R.

We show R* is an iterator relation for (W,c,g).

First, (1,c) is in R* because every R in I is an iterator relation, and by definition an iterator relation contains (1,c).

Now let x in R* be arbitrary, say x = (n,w). Since (n,w) is in R* and every R in I is an iterator relation, (n,w) is in each R in I. Hence, for each R in I,
    (S(n), g(w)) is in R.
Therefore
    (S(n), g(w)) is in R*.

Hence R* is an iterator relation for (W,c,g).

# Maximum Implies Supremum

Canonical theorem label: `prop:maximum-implies-supremum`

## OCR Text

## Polished Markdown

Suppose $m$ is a maximum of $A$. Then $m\in A$ and
$$
x\le m
$$
for every $x\in A$. Hence $m$ is an upper bound of $A$.

Now let $u$ be any upper bound of $A$. Since $m\in A$, the upper-bound
property of $u$ gives $m\le u$. Thus every upper bound $u$ of $A$
satisfies $m\le u$. Therefore $m$ is the least upper bound of $A$, so
$$
m=\sup A.
$$

prop:maximum-implies-supremum.title: Maximum Implies Supremum (proof-2026-07-31-002)
prop:maximum-implies-supremum.body:
Correct proof: if m=max A then m is an upper bound of A, and the maximum element m itself witnesses the epsilon-near-supremum condition, so m=sup A.

Tags: handwritten, correct, staging
prop:maximum-implies-supremum.ocr_text:
Thm: If set A has a maximum then max A = sup A.

Let A be a set with maximum.

m = max A, so a <= m for all a in A.

By definition of upper bound, m is an upper bound of A.

Let epsilon > 0 be arbitrary. Then there exists an a in A such that
m - epsilon < a <= m.

Since m in A, let a = m. Therefore
m - epsilon < m <= m.

Hence m is the least upper bound, and
max A = sup A.

Let l be any other lower bound for A.
Then l <= a for all a in A.

Since m in A, l <= m.
Therefore m is the greatest lower bound, and min A = inf A.

prop:minimum-implies-infimum.tex:
Thm: If set A has a minimum, then min A = inf A.

Assume A is a set with a minimum.

Let m = min A. Then m <= a for all a in A.
Therefore m is a lower bound of A.

Let l be any other lower bound for A.
Then l <= a for all a in A.

Since m in A, l <= m.
Therefore m is the greatest lower bound, and min A = inf A.

Correct handwritten proof of the supremum upper-bound characterization: shows the supremum is an upper bound and no smaller number can be an upper bound, and conversely these two properties characterize the supremum.

Tags: handwritten-proof, verified, supremum, bounds
prop:upper-bound-comparison-with-the-sup.ocr_text:
Abbott 1.2.8.
Let A be bounded above. Show that s = sup A iff:
1. s is an upper bound of A;
2. no smaller number is an upper bound of A.

Proof.
Assume s = sup A. Then by definition of the supremum, s is an upper bound of A and s is the least upper bound. Hence no smaller number is an upper bound.

Conversely, assume s is an upper bound of A and no smaller number is an upper bound of A.
Then s >= a for every a in A.
Since no smaller number is an upper bound of A, s is the least upper bound of A.
Therefore s = sup A.

thm:addition-commutative.body:
Incomplete attempt: uses induction to prove addition commutativity, but the base case is not properly established from the recursive definition, and the inductive step assumes successor manipulation/injectivity without proving the needed auxiliary identities.

Tags: handwritten, incorrect-attempt, staging
thm:addition-commutative.ocr_text:
Project Landau.

Thm. Addition on natural numbers is commutative:
  x + y = y + x for all x,y in N.

Proof. Fix x in N. We proceed by induction on N.

Base case:
  x + 1 = 1 + x.

Inductive hypothesis:
  x + y = y + x.

Show:
  x + y + 1 = y + x + 1
  x + y' = y + x'
  (x + y)' = (y + x)'
  (x + y)' = (x + y)' by inductive hypothesis.

If two successors are equal, then their bases are equal.
Therefore addition is commutative.

thm:algebra-of-lipschitz-functions.body:
Partial attempt: correctly proves the sum and scalar-multiple Lipschitz estimates, but the theorem also includes product and max/min parts; the product statement needs boundedness hypotheses and the remaining cases are not proved on this page.

Tags: handwritten, incorrect-attempt, partial, staging
thm:algebra-of-lipschitz-functions.ocr_text:
Continuity proofs.

Thm. Algebra of Lipschitz functions.
Let f,g : I -> R be Lipschitz with constants K_f, K_g. Then:

1. Sum: f + g is Lipschitz with constant K_f + K_g.
2. Scalar multiple: cf is Lipschitz with constant |c| K_f.
3. Product: fg is Lipschitz with constant K_f |g|, provided f and g are
   bounded.
4. Max/min: max(f,g) and min(f,g) are Lipschitz with constant max(K_f,K_g).

Proof.
1. We have
  |f(x) - f(u)| <= K_f |x-u|,
  |g(x) - g(u)| <= K_g |x-u|.
Adding these yields
  |f(x)-f(u)| + |g(x)-g(u)| <= (K_f + K_g)|x-u|,
so
  |(f+g)(x) - (f+g)(u)| <= (K_f + K_g)|x-u|.

2. We have
  |f(x)-f(u)| <= K_f |x-u|.
Then
  |cf(x) - cf(u)| = |c| |f(x)-f(u)| <= |c| K_f |x-u|.

Thm: Function Congruence
If x=y then f(x)=f(y)
\forall x \forall y (x=y -> f(x)=f(y))

Proof: Assume x=y. By reflexivity x=x.
x=x. f(x)=f(x) by reflexivity.
Let phi(z) := f(x)=f(z).
Since x=y, phi(x) <-> phi(y).
Since phi(x) = f(x)=f(x),
phi(y) = f(x)=f(y).
Hence if x=y then f(x)=f(y).
thm:axiomatic-equality-function-congruen.markdown:
# Function Congruence

Canonical theorem label: `thm:axiomatic-equality-function-congruence`

## OCR Text

Thm: Function Congruence
If x=y then f(x)=f(y)
\forall x \forall y (x=y -> f(x)=f(y))

Proof: Assume x=y. By reflexivity x=x.
x=x. f(x)=f(x) by reflexivity.
Let phi(z) := f(x)=f(z).
Since x=y, phi(x) <-> phi(y).
Since phi(x) = f(x)=f(x),
phi(y) = f(x)=f(y).
Hence if x=y then f(x)=f(y).

## Polished Markdown

Assume $x=y$. By reflexivity of equality, $f(x)=f(x)$. Let $\Phi(z)$
be the formula $f(x)=f(z)$. Then $\Phi(x)$ holds. Since $x=y$,
substitution of identicals applied to the formula-context $\Phi$ gives
$\Phi(y)$. Hence $f(x)=f(y)$. Therefore $x=y\to f(x)=f(y)$, and
universal generalization gives
$$
\forall x\,\forall y\,(x=y\to f(x)=f(y)).
$$

## Polished TeX

be the formula \(f(x)=f(z)\). Then \(\Phi(x)\) holds. Since \(x=y\),
substitution of identicals applied to the formula-context \(\Phi\) gives

universal generalization gives
\[

\]

Canonical theorem label: `thm:axiomatic-equality-transitivity`

## OCR Text

Thm: Transitivity of Equality

If x = y and y = z then x = z

For all x, for all y, for all z,
((x = y and y = z) -> x = z)

Proof: Assume hypothesis, x = y and y = z.

Substitute z for y in x = y, because y = z.

x = z and y = z.

Hence x = z as desired.

Therefore if x = y and y = z then x = z.

## Polished Markdown

Assume $x=y$ and $y=z$. Let $\Phi(w)$ be the formula $x=w$. From the
first assumption, $\Phi(y)$ holds. From the second assumption and
substitution of identicals applied to the formula-context $\Phi$, it follows
that $\Phi(z)$ holds. Hence $x=z$. Therefore
$(x=y\land y=z)\to x=z$, and universal generalization gives
$$
\forall x\,\forall y\,\forall z\,\bigl((x=y\land y=z)\to x=z\bigr).
$$

thm:bezout-identity-on-z.ocr_text:
Abstract Algebra proof.

Thm. Let a,b be integers. Then the greatest common divisor d = gcd(a,b)
is an integer combination of a,b. There exist m and n in Z such that
  d = ma + nb.

Assume d = gcd(a,b).

If a,b = 0 then d = 0 and any n,m satisfies the linear combination requirement.

Assume a or b != 0.
Define S := {ma + nb | ma + nb > 0}.
S is nonempty; consider m = a and n = b, so a^2 + b^2 is in S.

Therefore by the well-ordering principle there is a least element. We define
d as this element.

Claim: d | a and d | b, and if c | a and c | b then c | d for c in Z.

Use the division algorithm:
  a = dq + r
  r = a - q(ma + nb)
  r = a(1 - qm) + b(-nq).

Therefore r is a linear combination of a,b. However, r not in S because
0 <= r < d would mean that r < d, contradicting that d is the least element.

thm:bolzano-weierstrass-sequences.title: Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem for Sequences (proof-2026-07-31-001)
thm:bolzano-weierstrass-sequences.body:
Correct proof idea: every real sequence has a monotone subsequence; a bounded monotone subsequence converges by the monotone convergence theorem, giving a convergent subsequence of the original bounded sequence.

Tags: handwritten, correct, staging
thm:bolzano-weierstrass-sequences.ocr_text:
Thm. Bolzano-Weierstrass. Every bounded sequence in R has a convergent subsequence.

Let (x_n) be a bounded sequence. Then there exists M such that |x_n| <= M
for every n.

By the monotone subsequence theorem, (x_n) has a monotone subsequence (x_{n_k}).
Without loss of generality, suppose this subsequence is increasing. Since it is
a subsequence of a bounded sequence, it is bounded above by M.

By the monotone convergence theorem, the bounded increasing subsequence converges.
The decreasing case is analogous, using the lower bound.

Therefore (x_n) has a convergent subsequence.

thm:cauchy-sequence-with-convergent-subs.title: Cauchy Sequence with a Convergent Subsequence (proof-2026-07-31-001)
thm:cauchy-sequence-with-convergent-subs.body:
Correct proof: uses convergence of a subsequence to L and the Cauchy property to make |x_n-x_{n_k}| and |x_{n_k}-L| small, then applies the triangle inequality to show x_n -> L.

Tags: handwritten, correct, staging
thm:cauchy-sequence-with-convergent-subs.ocr_text:
Thm. Cauchy sequences converge.

Let x_n be a Cauchy sequence. By Bolzano, x_{n_k} is a convergent subsequence
and x_{n_k} -> L.

Then there exists N_k such that for all n >= N_k,
  |x_{n_k} - L| < epsilon/2.  (1)

Since x_n is Cauchy,
  |x_n - x_{n_k}| < epsilon/2.  (2)

Combine (1) and (2):
  |x_n - L| <= |x_n - x_{n_k}| + |x_{n_k} - L| < epsilon.

Therefore the Cauchy sequence converges.
thm:cauchy-sequence-with-convergent-subs.markdown:
# Cauchy Sequence with a Convergent Subsequence

Canonical theorem label: `thm:cauchy-sequence-with-convergent-subsequence`

## OCR Text

Thm. Cauchy sequences converge.

Let x_n be a Cauchy sequence. By Bolzano, x_{n_k} is a convergent subsequence
and x_{n_k} -> L.

Then there exists N_k such that for all n >= N_k,
  |x_{n_k} - L| < epsilon/2.  (1)

Since x_n is Cauchy,
  |x_n - x_{n_k}| < epsilon/2.  (2)

Thm. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy.

Let x_n be a convergent sequence with x_n -> L.
Let epsilon > 0. Since x_n -> L, there exists N in N such that for all n >= N,

  < epsilon/2 + epsilon/2
  = epsilon.

Therefore (x_n) is Cauchy.

thm:empty-set-exists-unique.ocr_text:
Thm: Existence and uniqueness of Empty Set

There exists a unique set E such that no object is an element of E.

exists! E forall x (x notin E)

Proof: By the Axiom of the empty set there exists a set E with no elements.

E := {x : x notin E}

Let F be a set satisfying the empty set.

To show E is unique must show E = F. By Axiom of Extensionality, to show E = F
iff E and F have the same members.

Case => forall x (x in E -> x in F) is true because x in E is false.

Case <= forall x (x in F -> x in E) is true because x in F is false.

Therefore E = F as desired.
thm:empty-set-exists-unique.markdown:
# Existence and Uniqueness of the Empty Set

Canonical theorem label: `thm:empty-set-exists-unique`

## OCR Text

Thm: Existence and uniqueness of Empty Set

There exists a unique set E such that no object is an element of E.

exists! E forall x (x notin E)

Proof: By the Axiom of the empty set there exists a set E with no elements.

E := {x : x notin E}

Let F be a set satisfying the empty set.

To show E is unique must show E = F. By Axiom of Extensionality, to show E = F
iff E and F have the same members.

Case => forall x (x in E -> x in F) is true because x in E is false.

Case <= forall x (x in F -> x in E) is true because x in F is false.

Therefore E = F as desired.

## Polished Markdown

By the Axiom of Empty Set, there is a set $E$ such that
$$
\forall x,\ x\notin E.
$$
It remains to prove uniqueness. Let $F$ be any set such that
$$
\forall x,\ x\notin F.
$$
For every object $x$, the implications $x\in E\to x\in F$ and
$x\in F\to x\in E$ are true, since their antecedents are false. Hence
$$
\forall x,\ (x\in E\leftrightarrow x\in F).
$$
By the Axiom of Extensionality, $E=F$. Therefore there exists a unique set
with no elements.

Then inf(A-B) = infA - supB.

lb ≤ a for all a ∈ A
lb ≤ -b for all b ∈ B
la + ib ≤ a - b for all a ∈ A and b ∈ B
Therefore la + ib is a lower bound of A-B.

## Polished Markdown

Let
$$
i_A=\inf A
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
s_B=\sup B.
$$
For every $a\in A$ and $b\in B$, the definitions of infimum and supremum give
$$
i_A\le a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
b\le s_B.
$$
Hence $-s_B\le -b$, and therefore
$$
i_A-s_B\le a-b.
$$
Thus $i_A-s_B$ is a lower bound for $A-B$.

It remains to show that this lower bound is greatest. Let $\varepsilon>0$. By
the epsilon characterization of the infimum, there exists $a_\varepsilon\in A$
such that
$$
a_\varepsilon<i_A+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
$$
By the epsilon characterization of the supremum, there exists
$b_\varepsilon\in B$ such that
$$
s_B-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}<b_\varepsilon.
$$
Subtracting the second estimate from the first gives
$$
a_\varepsilon-b_\varepsilon
<
i_A-s_B+\varepsilon.
$$
Since $a_\varepsilon-b_\varepsilon\in A-B$, every positive epsilon produces an
element of $A-B$ below $i_A-s_B+\varepsilon$. Together with the lower-bound
property already proved, the epsilon characterization of the infimum gives
$$
\inf(A-B)=i_A-s_B=\inf A-\sup B.
$$

Theorem. Monotonicity of infimum.
If A subset B, then inf B <= inf A.

Let i_b = inf B.

Thm: Infimum <= Supremum
Let A subset R be nonempty, bounded below and bounded above. Then inf A <= sup A.

Proof:
Let x in A be arbitrary. Then by definition of the infimum and supremum:
inf A <= x,
x <= sup A.

Because $A$ is nonempty, choose $x\in A$. Since $\inf A$ is a lower
bound of $A$, we have
$$
\inf A\le x.
$$
Since $\sup A$ is an upper bound of $A$, we have
$$
x\le \sup A.
$$
By transitivity of the order on $\mathbb{R}$,
$$
\inf A\le \sup A.
$$

thm:infimum-sum-set.body:
Handwritten proof photo supplied by user for Volume III infimum of a sum set.

Tags: handwritten, volume-iii, infimum-sum-set
thm:infimum-sum-set.ocr_text:
Thm: Infimum of Sum Set

Let \( A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R} \) be non-empty and bounded below. Then
\[ \inf(A + B) = \inf A + \inf B. \]

Proof: Let \( i_A := \inf A \), \( i_B := \inf B \)

\[ i_A \leq a \text{ for all } a \in A \]
\[ i_B \leq b \text{ for all } b \in B \]

\[ i_A + i_B \leq a + b \text{ for all } a \in A, b \in B. \]

Therefore \( i_A + i_B \) is a lower bound of \( A + B \).

Let \( \varepsilon > 0 \) be arbitrary, then

\[ a_\varepsilon + b_\varepsilon < i_A + i_B + \varepsilon \text{ for some } a \in A, b \in B \]

\[ a_\varepsilon < i_A + \frac{\varepsilon}{2}, \quad b_\varepsilon < i_B + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \]

\[ i_A < a_\varepsilon < i_A + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \quad i_B < b_\varepsilon < i_B + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \]

\[ i_A + i_B < i_A + i_B + \varepsilon \]

Since \( b_\varepsilon \in A + B \) is a lower bound of \( A + B \), the infimum of \( A + B \) is \( i_A + i_B \).

Therefore \( \inf(A + B) = \inf A + \inf B \).

Correct alternate proof of the infimum sum-set theorem: establishes inf A + inf B as a lower bound of A+B, then uses epsilon/2 witnesses near each infimum to force inf(A+B) <= inf A + inf B.

thm:infimum-sum-set.ocr_text:
Thm: Additivity of infimum.
Let A and B be nonempty sets of real numbers that are bounded below.
Define the sum of the sets as
A+B := {a+b : a in A, b in B}.
Then inf(A+B) = inf A + inf B.

Let i_a = inf A, i_b = inf B, and i_ab = inf(A+B).

i_a is a lower bound for A.
i_b is a lower bound for B.
i_ab is a lower bound for A+B.

Let epsilon > 0 be arbitrary. Since i_a and i_b are infima, there exist
a in A and b in B such that
a < i_a + epsilon/2
and
b < i_b + epsilon/2.

Since a+b is in A+B,
i_ab <= a+b < i_a+i_b+epsilon.

Also adding the lower-bound inequalities gives
i_a+i_b <= a+b for every a in A and b in B, so i_a+i_b is a lower bound of A+B.
Thus i_a+i_b <= i_ab.

Therefore inf(A+B) = inf A + inf B.

Then (a_n + b_n) -> a + b.

Let epsilon > 0. Since a_n -> a, there exists N_1 in N such that for all n >= N_1,
|a_n - a| < epsilon/2.

Since b_n -> b, there exists N_2 in N such that for all n >= N_2,
|b_n - b| < epsilon/2.

|(a_n + b_n) - (a + b)|

  <= |a_n - a| + |b_n - b|
  < epsilon/2 + epsilon/2
  = epsilon.

Therefore a_n + b_n -> a + b.

thm:lub-property-implies-existence-of-su.ocr_text:
Assume A is nonempty and bounded above, then sup A exists.

B = { b in A^c | b is upper bound of A }.

B is bounded below by A.
For all a in A and for all b in B, a <= b.

Let epsilon be arbitrary. If b - epsilon >= a, then b - epsilon would be an upper bound of A and be in B.
Therefore b - epsilon < a.

Since b is an upper bound and b - epsilon < a, b is a supremum of A.

Therefore, if A is nonempty and bounded above, A has a supremum.

We prove by structural induction on $\varphi\in\WFF$ that
$\varphi\in S$.

If $\varphi$ is atomic, then $\varphi=P$ for some
$P\in\Prop$. Since $\Prop\subseteq S$, it follows that
$\varphi=P\in S$.

Suppose $\varphi=\neg\theta$, where $\theta\in\WFF$. By the induction
hypothesis, $\theta\in S$. By the second hypothesis on $S$,
$\neg\theta\in S$. Hence $\varphi\in S$.

Suppose $\varphi=(\theta\circ\psi)$, where
$\theta,\psi\in\WFF$ and
$$
\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\}.
$$
By the induction hypothesis, $\theta\in S$ and $\psi\in S$. By the
third hypothesis on $S$, $(\theta\circ\psi)\in S$. Hence
$\varphi\in S$.

Therefore every $\varphi\in\WFF$ belongs to $S$, and so
$$
\WFF\subseteq S.
$$

Let x_n be a bounded-above increasing sequence. Then for all n, x_n <= M.
Define S = {x_i : i in N}. Because x_n is bounded above, S is bounded above
and has a supremum.

Let s = sup S. For every epsilon > 0, there exists an element of S with
s - epsilon < x_N <= s.
Since the sequence is increasing, for all n >= N,
s - epsilon < x_N <= x_n <= s < s + epsilon.

Thus |x_n - s| < epsilon for all n >= N, so x_n -> s.

thm:monotone-subsequence-theorem.title: Monotone Subsequence Theorem (proof-2026-07-31-001)
thm:monotone-subsequence-theorem.body:
Correct peak argument proof: if there are infinitely many peaks, the peak subsequence is monotone decreasing; if there are finitely many peaks, recursively choose later non-peak indices to build a monotone increasing subsequence.

Tags: handwritten, correct, staging
thm:monotone-subsequence-theorem.ocr_text:
Thm. Monotone subsequence theorem. Every sequence in R has a monotone subsequence.

Let (x_n) be a sequence in R.
Define a peak as an index m such that x_m >= x_n for all n >= m.

Case 1: There are infinitely many peaks. Record the sequence of peak indices
m_1 < m_2 < ... . Since each m_i is a peak, x_{m_i} >= x_{m_j} whenever j > i.
Thus (x_{m_i}) is a decreasing subsequence.

Case 2: There are only finitely many peaks. Let m be the index of the last peak
and set k_1 = m + 1. Since k_1 is not a peak, there exists k_2 > k_1 such that
x_{k_2} >= x_{k_1}. Repeating the process, construct indices
k_1 < k_2 < ... with x_{k_{j+1}} >= x_{k_j}.
Thus (x_{k_j}) is an increasing subsequence.

Therefore every real sequence has a monotone subsequence.

## Polished Markdown

Let $i=\inf A$. We prove that $-i$ is the supremum of $-A$.

First let $y\in -A$. Then $y=-x$ for some $x\in A$. Since $i$ is a
lower bound of $A$, we have $i\le x$. Multiplying by $-1$ reverses the
inequality, so
$$
y=-x\le -i.
$$
Thus $-i$ is an upper bound of $-A$. In particular, $-A$ is bounded
above.

Now let $u$ be any upper bound of $-A$. For every $x\in A$, the element
$-x$ belongs to $-A$, so
$$
-x\le u.
$$
Multiplying by $-1$ gives
$$
-u\le x
$$
for every $x\in A$. Hence $-u$ is a lower bound of $A$. Since $i=\inf A$
is the greatest lower bound of $A$, we have $-u\le i$. Multiplying by
$-1$ again gives
$$
-i\le u.
$$
Therefore every upper bound $u$ of $-A$ lies above $-i$. Since $-i$ is
itself an upper bound of $-A$, it is the least upper bound of $-A$. Hence
$$
\sup(-A)=-i=-\inf A.
$$

thm:negation-exchange-sup-inf.tex:
Bound proofs.

Thm. Negation exchanges supremum and infimum.
Let A subset R be a nonempty set. If A is bounded below, then
-A := {-a | a in A}
is bounded above and
sup(-A) = -inf A.

Proof. Let i_A = inf A. Since A is nonempty and bounded below, inf A exists.

For all a in A,
i_A <= a.  (1)

Multiplying by -1 gives
-i_A >= -a.  (2)

Let s_A = sup(-A). Then s_A >= -a for all a in A.
Therefore -i_A is an upper bound of -A.

The page concludes that -i_A is the least upper bound of -A, hence
sup(-A) = -inf A.

thm:no-object-is-its-own-successor.title: No Object Is Its Own Successor (proof-2026-07-31-002)
thm:no-object-is-its-own-successor.body:
Handwritten induction proof that no Peano-system object is its own successor. Defines D={x in P | S(x) != x}, proves the base case from the Peano base-not-successor axiom, and uses successor injectivity for the induction step. Correct.

Tags: handwritten, peano-system, induction
thm:no-object-is-its-own-successor.ocr_text:
Theorem. No object is its own successor.
Let (P,S,1) be a Peano system. For every n in P, S(n) != n.

Proof.
Define
    D := {x in P | S(x) != x}.

Proceed by induction.

Base case:
1 is in D because 1 is in P and S(1) != 1.

Induction step:
Assume n is in D, so S(n) != n.
By the contrapositive of the Peano injectivity of successors, if S(n) != n, then
    S(S(n)) != S(n).
Hence S(n) is in D.

Therefore D = P, so for every n in P, S(n) != n.

thm:one-plus-n.ocr_text:
Project Landau.

Lemma. The successor lemma is commutative:
  x + 1 = 1 + x.

Proof. Let x be arbitrary in N. We proceed by induction.

Base case:
  1 + 1 = 1 + 1.

Inductive hypothesis:
  x + 1 = 1 + x.

Show:
  x + 1 + 1 = 1 + x + 1
  (x + 1)' = (1 + x)'.
By the inductive hypothesis,
  (1 + x)' = (1 + x)'.

If d' = d' then d = d.
Therefore x + 1 = 1 + x and successor is commutative.

thm:polynomial-sequence-limit.title: Polynomial Sequence Limit (proof-2026-07-31-001)
thm:polynomial-sequence-limit.body:
Correct proof sketch: treats a polynomial as a finite linear combination of powers; uses repeated multiplication to get x_n^m -> L^m from x_n -> L, scalar multiples for coefficients, and finite sums by the algebra of sequence limits.

Tags: handwritten, correct, staging
thm:polynomial-sequence-limit.ocr_text:
Theorem: Limit of a polynomial sequence.

If x_n -> x and p is a polynomial, then p(x_n) -> p(x).

Consider an arbitrary polynomial
  A x_n^m + B x_n^{m-1} + ... + C x_n + D.

Exponentiation is repeated multiplication:
  x_n^m = x_n x_n ... x_n, m times.

Since A x_n -> A x and x_n^m -> x^m for all m, by the algebra of sequences
it can be seen that p(x_n) -> p(x).

# Scalar Multiplication by a Negative Scalar

Canonical theorem label: `thm:scalar-mult-negative`

## Polished Markdown

Let $N=-k$. Since $k<0$, we have $N>0$. Also
$$
kA=\{ka:a\in A\}=\{N(-a):a\in A\}=N(-A).
$$
Because $A$ is bounded below, $-A$ is bounded above. By scalar multiplication
by a positive scalar,
$$
\sup(N(-A))=N\sup(-A).
$$
By negation exchanging supremum and infimum,
$$
\sup(-A)=-\inf A.
$$
Therefore
$$
\sup(kA)=\sup(N(-A))=N\sup(-A)=N(-\inf A)=-N\inf A.
$$
Since $N=-k$, we have $-N=k$. Hence
$$
\sup(kA)=k\inf A.
$$

thm:scalar-mult-negative.title: Scalar Multiplication by a Negative Scalar (proof-2026-07-31-002)
thm:scalar-mult-negative.body:
Incorrect attempt: target is sup(cA)=c inf A for c<0, but the epsilon choice uses epsilon/c with c<0, which moves below the infimum rather than above it, and the final inequality chain does not establish the supremum equality.

Tags: handwritten, needs-revision, staging
thm:scalar-mult-negative.ocr_text:
Thm. Let c < 0. If A is bounded above, then sup(cA) = c inf A.

Let s_a = sup(cA), so ca <= s_a for all a in A.
Let i_a = inf A, so i_a <= a for all a in A.

Let epsilon > 0 be arbitrary. Then there exists a in A such that
a < i_a + epsilon/c.

Multiplying by c, noting c < 0, gives
epsilon + c i_a < c a.

Also ca <= s_a.
Thus c i_a < c a <= s_a.

Since ca is in cA and ca <= s_a, the attempt concludes
s_a <= c i_a <= s_a, hence sup(cA) = c inf A.

Review note: the epsilon choice has the wrong sign for c < 0 and the final inequality
chain does not establish the claimed equality.

Let $s=\sup A$. By definition of supremum, $a\le s$ for all $a\in A$.
Since $k>0$, multiplying preserves the order, so $ka\le ks$ for all
$a\in A$. Hence $ks$ is an upper bound of $kA$.

Let $t=\sup(kA)$. Since $ks$ is an upper bound of $kA$, the least-upper-bound
property gives
$$
t\le ks.
$$
Since $t$ is an upper bound of $kA$, we have $ka\le t$ for all $a\in A$.
Because $k>0$, dividing by $k$ preserves the order, so
$$
a\le \frac{t}{k}
$$
for all $a\in A$. Thus $t/k$ is an upper bound of $A$. Since $s=\sup A$,
$$
s\le \frac{t}{k}.
$$
Multiplying again by $k>0$, we get
$$
ks\le t.
$$
Together with $t\le ks$, this gives $t=ks$. Therefore
$$
\sup(kA)=k\sup A.
$$

thm:scalar-mult-positive.ocr_text:
Thm. Let c > 0 be a constant. If A is bounded above, then
sup(cA) = c sup A,
where cA := {ca : a in A}.

Let s_a = sup A, so s_a >= a for all a in A.
Let s_ac = sup(cA), so s_ac >= ca for all a in A.

a <= s_a <= s_ac.
ca <= c s_a <= s_ac.
Thus s_ac is an upper bound.

Let epsilon be arbitrary. Then
s_ac < ca - epsilon/c.
Since that cannot happen, s_ac is the supremum of c s_a.

c s_a - epsilon < c(a - epsilon/c) < ca, with ca in cA.

Therefore s_ac is the least upper bound.
Therefore sup(cA) = c sup A.

Since the image of the function x_{n_k} is bounded between [a,b], L must be
between [a,b].

Therefore the limit of the subsequence is in [a,b].

thm:sign-of-reciprocal-q.ocr_text:
Rational Proofs

Thm: Inverse Positive.
If a > 0, then a^{-1} > 0 for all a in Q with a != 0.

Proof:
a > 0
a . a^{-1} > 0 . a^{-1}
a . a^{-1} > 0
1 > 0

By trichotomy, a^{-1} must be exactly one of these:
a^{-1} = 0 or a^{-1} > 0 or a^{-1} < 0.

Since a^{-1} = 1/a and we know a > 0,
a^{-1} != 0 and a^{-1} not < 0, therefore
a^{-1} > 0.

Let $s=\sup A$ and $i=\inf A$.

If $\lambda=0$, then $\lambda A=\{0\}$ because $A$ is nonempty. Hence
$$
\sup(\lambda A)=0=\max\{0s,0i\}.
$$

If $\lambda>0$, the positive scalar multiplication theorem gives
$$
\sup(\lambda A)=\lambda\sup A=\lambda s.
$$
Since $i\le s$ and $\lambda>0$, we have $\lambda i\le \lambda s$, so
$$
\max\{\lambda s,\lambda i\}=\lambda s=\sup(\lambda A).
$$

If $\lambda<0$, the negative scalar multiplication theorem gives
$$
\sup(\lambda A)=\lambda\inf A=\lambda i.
$$
Since $i\le s$ and multiplication by the negative scalar $\lambda$ reverses
order, $\lambda s\le \lambda i$. Therefore
$$
\max\{\lambda s,\lambda i\}=\lambda i=\sup(\lambda A).
$$

The three cases cover every real value of $\lambda$, so
$$
\sup(\lambda A)=\max\{\lambda\sup A,\lambda\inf A\}.
$$

thm:supremum-is-monotone-under-inclusion.ocr_text:
Theorem. If A subset B, then sup A <= sup B.

Proof.
Let A and B be sets with A subset B.
Let s_a = sup A and s_b = sup B.

For every a in A, since A subset B, a is in B.
Thus a <= s_b for every a in A, so s_b is an upper bound of A.

Since s_a is the least upper bound of A,
    s_a <= s_b.

Thm. Let A and B be nonempty subsets of R that are bounded above.
Define A+B := {a+b : a in A, b in B}. Then
sup(A+B) = sup A + sup B.

Let s_a = sup A, s_b = sup B, and s_ab = sup(A+B).

a <= s_a for all a in A, and b <= s_b for all b in B.
Thus s_a+s_b is an upper bound of A+B.

For all a in A and b in B, a+b <= s_ab.
Also a+b <= s_a+s_b, so s_ab <= s_a+s_b.

Therefore s_ab = s_a+s_b, and
sup(A+B) = sup(A)+sup(B).

thm:tail-equality-preserves-convergence.title: Tail Equality Preserves Convergence (proof-2026-07-31-001)
thm:tail-equality-preserves-convergence.body:
Correct proof idea: if two sequences differ only in finitely many terms, then after the last differing index they are identical, so their tails and convergence tests agree with the same limit.

Tags: handwritten, correct, staging
thm:tail-equality-preserves-convergence.ocr_text:
Thm. If two sequences x_n and y_n differ in only finitely many terms, then either
both converge to the same value or neither converges.

Define S = {n in N : x_n != y_n}.
If S is empty, then x_n = y_n for every n.
If S is nonempty, let N = max S.

Past N, x_n = y_n. Therefore for all n >= N, the sequences have identical tails.
Hence the convergence tests for the tails are identical.

Therefore either both sequences converge to the same limit, or neither sequence converges.

thm:tail-suprema-are-decreasing.body:
Correct proof sketch: defines the tail supremum sequence s_n = sup{x_k:k >= n}; since each later tail is a subset of the earlier tail, s_{n+1} <= s_n, so the tail suprema are decreasing. Notes the analogous argument for tail infima.

Tags: handwritten, correct, staging
thm:tail-suprema-are-decreasing.ocr_text:
Thm. limsup / liminf.

Let (x_n) be a bounded sequence. Define
  a_n := sup {x_k | k >= n},
  b_n := inf {x_k | k >= n}.

1. The sequence (a_n) is bounded monotone decreasing.
   The sequence (b_n) is bounded monotone increasing.
   Therefore liminf x_n and limsup x_n exist.

2. limsup x_n = inf {a_n | n in N}.
   liminf x_n = sup {b_n | n in N}.

3. liminf x_n <= limsup x_n.

The sequence a_n is bounded because x_n is bounded. It is monotone decreasing
because a_n excludes the current supremum every time n increases.

Inductive argument. Base case k = 1:
  a_{n_k} := sup {x_k | k >= 1}.
By definition of supremum, a_{n_k} >= x_k for all n in N.

Inductive base: assume a_j = sup {x_{n_j} | k >= j}. Then
  a_{n_k} >= a_{n_j}.

Show j+1:
  a_{n_{j+1}} = sup {x_{n_{j+1}} | k >= j+1}.
Thus a_{n_{j+1}} <= a_{n_j}.

Since a_{n_k} >= a_{n_{k+1}} for all n in N, a_n is monotone decreasing and
limsup x_n exists.

Similar argument can be made for liminf.

thm:translation-invariance-supremum.body:
Correct alternate proof of translation invariance: sup A + c is an upper bound of A+c, giving sup(A+c) <= sup A + c; then sup(A+c)-c is an upper bound of A, giving sup A + c <= sup(A+c).

Tags: handwritten, correct, alternate, duplicate-family, staging
thm:translation-invariance-supremum.ocr_text:
Let c in R. Prove that sup(A+c) = sup A + c.

s_a = sup A, so a <= s_a for all a in A.

a+c <= s_a+c for all a in A.

s_c = sup(A+c), so a+c <= s_c for all a in A.

s_a+c is an upper bound of A+c, hence
s_c <= s_a+c.

Also a+c <= s_c, so
a <= s_c-c.
Thus s_c-c is an upper bound of A.

Since s_a is sup A, s_a <= s_c-c, so
s_a+c <= s_c.

Hence sup(A+c) = sup A+c.

thm:unbounded-monotone-divergence.ocr_text:
Thm. Monotone unbounded sequences diverge.

Let x_n be a monotone sequence that is unbounded.
Since x_n is unbounded, there exists an M such that for any n,
  |x_n| > M.

Therefore, if x_n is monotone increasing, the sequence will exceed any
arbitrary value. For a decreasing sequence, the sequence will be smaller
than any arbitrary value.

Therefore an unbounded monotone sequence diverges as follows:
  x_n -> +infinity, if x_n is increasing;
  x_n -> -infinity, if x_n is decreasing.

Correct handwritten proof of uniqueness of sequence limits using epsilon = |L1-L2|/2 and the triangle inequality after both tail estimates hold.

thm:uniqueness-of-limits.ocr_text:
Theorem. If a sequence (a_n) converges, its limit is unique.

Proof.
Assume (a_n) converges to L1 and also to L2.
Let epsilon > 0, and take epsilon = |L1 - L2|/2.
There exists N1 such that for n >= N1,
    |a_n - L1| < epsilon.
There exists N2 such that for n >= N2,
    |a_n - L2| < epsilon.

For n >= max(N1,N2), both estimates hold. By the triangle inequality,
    |L1 - L2| <= |L1 - a_n| + |a_n - L2| < 2 epsilon.
With epsilon = |L1 - L2|/2, this forces |L1 - L2| = 0.
Therefore L1 = L2.

thm:uniqueness-of-limits.ocr_text:
Theorem. If a sequence (a_n) converges, its limit is unique.

Proof.
Assume (a_n) is a convergent sequence that converges to L1.
Further assume a_n also converges to L2.
Let epsilon > 0, chosen as |L1 - L2|/2.
Then there exists N1 such that for n >= N1,
    |a_n - L1| < epsilon.
There also exists N2 such that for n >= N2,
    |a_n - L2| < epsilon.

Choose n >= max(N1,N2). Then
    |L1 - L2| = |L1 - a_n + a_n - L2|
        <= |L1 - a_n| + |a_n - L2|
        < 2 epsilon.
Taking epsilon = |L1 - L2|/2 gives |L1 - L2| = 0.
Therefore L1 and L2 are the same point.
